metadata.title: Exploring complex problem-solving in vietnamese students: An investigation of performance data and process data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary data from 589 undergraduate students at a single university in southern Vietnam using an online CPS test administered in university computer rooms. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey design weights (e.g., sampling weights or replicate weights) or any weight variable names, and the analysis is based on this convenience sample rather than an international representative ILSA sample. Because no PV-based achievement scores from PISA were analyzed (the CPS scores were Rasch-scaled from dichotomous items), standard ILSA weight guidance is not directly applicable. For replication or extension with representative samples, analysts should apply the appropriate sampling weights from the underlying study design (if available) and consider clustering by classroom/school; however, the current paper provides no such weighting details.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are Rasch-scaled CPS scores derived from dichotomous item scoring and process-data indicators (e.g., number of interactions, time-on-task, strategy frequencies), not PISA-style Plausible Values (PV) achievement scores. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to this study’s scoring approach. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect Rasch estimation and correlations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 589 undergraduate students from a single university in southern Vietnam. Participation was voluntary and students had no prior experience with the MicroFIN/MicroDYN model-based simulation tasks. The CPS test consisted of one MicroFIN realistic simulation task (Robot Cleaner; six items) and three MicroDYN model-based simulation tasks (Air Conditioner Control, Social Activity, Basketball Training; each with six items total across tasks as described). The manuscript does not report additional exclusions (e.g., incomplete test sessions, missing responses) or any specific missing-data filtering rules.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroFIN Robot Cleaner; MicroDYN Air Conditioner Control, Social Activity, Basketball Training) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test (2023–2024 academic year, semester 1)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Paired t-test (phase difference): t(588)=7.33, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.31. Gender difference (overall): t(543.67)=3.569, p<.001, Cohen's d=0.30. Knowledge acquisition gender difference: t(516.32)=4.95, p<.001, Cohen's d=0.42. Knowledge application gender difference: p=.596, Cohen's d=0.05. Descriptive Rasch means: overall female Mean=-1.33 (SD=1.83) vs male Mean=-0.90 (SD=1.65).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from a Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test (MicroFIN Robot Cleaner and MicroDYN model-based tasks), the study compared CPS proficiency across gender and CPS phases, finding that male students scored higher than female students overall and particularly in the knowledge acquisition phase, while gender differences were not significant in knowledge application. This indicates that instructional support for exploration/knowledge acquisition strategies may be especially important for reducing gender-related gaps in complex problem-solving, though the study is correlational and does not use PV-based achievement or causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroDYN model-based tasks; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by number of actions
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model-based tasks: Pearson correlation between number of actions and knowledge acquisition achievement r=-0.087, p=0.04 (reported as negative/inefficient pattern). Gender difference in actions during knowledge acquisition: t(1855.5)=2.95, p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.14. Within model-based tasks, males tended to take fewer actions than females (directional statement; no additional effect size beyond the overall action gender test).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study examined how the number of interactions related to knowledge acquisition achievement in the MicroDYN model-based tasks, finding a small negative association (r=-0.087, p=0.04) suggesting that more actions did not necessarily translate into better exploration performance. This indicates that simply increasing engagement or interaction counts may not improve learning outcomes in model-based CPS; educators should instead teach efficient exploration strategies (e.g., control-of-variables/VOTAT) to convert effort into correct causal understanding.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroDYN model-based tasks; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by strategy type (Change 0–Change 3)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Strategy effectiveness correlations (Pearson r between frequency of strategy type and overall CPS achievement): Change 3 r=-0.213*** (all), Change 2 r=-0.150*** (all), Change 1 r=0.343*** (all), Change 0 r=-0.105* (all). Distribution of strategy use in exploratory phase: vary all three variables (Change 3) ~36% of observations; Change 2 ~19%; Change 0 ~15%; Change 1 (vary one variable) only ~30% of observations. Gender differences in strategy use: females more often varied two variables (Change 2) than males t(1544)=2.402, p=0.016, d=0.12; females had more Change 0 (no action) than males t(1566.7)=1.998, p=0.045, d=0.11; males more likely to apply Change 1 than females t(1090)=2.591, p=0.009, d=0.14.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study linked strategy type in MicroDYN model-based exploration to knowledge acquisition achievement and found that varying one variable at a time (Change 1/VOTAT) was positively associated with achievement (r=0.343***), whereas varying multiple variables simultaneously (Change 2/Change 3) and no-change behavior (Change 0) were negatively associated. This indicates that curriculum and instruction should explicitly train control-of-variables/VOTAT exploration routines, particularly for female students who showed higher rates of suboptimal strategies and observational passivity.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroDYN model-based tasks; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by spatial interaction bias (top-left preference)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Dispersion analysis results (no achievement correlation reported): top-left quadrant elements received more interactions; top-down interaction preference more pronounced in model-based simulation environment. Object interaction counts (exploration stage): Yellow 2129, Red 1683, Robot 1299, Green 1083, Blue 944. Dispersion metrics: Robot x-axis σ=3.61, IQR=6.3, CV=0.67; Green σ=2.81, IQR=4.0, CV=1.12; Red/Yellow/Blue σ≈2.8–3.1 with CV≈0.74–0.83.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study identified a pronounced habitual spatial scanning pattern in which students interacted more with interface elements in the top-left quadrant, with an even stronger top-down preference in model-based tasks. This indicates that assessment design and instruction should account for culturally shaped visual-spatial heuristics (e.g., top-left scanning) that may bias exploration away from functionally relevant variables, potentially undermining effective causal discovery.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroFIN realistic Robot Cleaner; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by number of actions
main_findings.performance_metrics: Realistic simulation task: Pearson correlation between number of actions and knowledge acquisition achievement r=0.198, p<0.001. Gender difference in actions during knowledge acquisition (Robot Cleaner): t(433.72)=5.36, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.48.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study analyzed the realistic MicroFIN Robot Cleaner task and found a positive association between the number of actions and knowledge acquisition achievement (r=0.198, p<0.001), with males taking more actions than females in this task. This indicates that in more realistic, less transparent environments, encouraging active exploration may support knowledge acquisition, but the effect depends on task structure and should be paired with strategy guidance rather than action-count targets.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroDYN and MicroFIN; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by time-on-task
main_findings.performance_metrics: Realistic simulation tasks: r=0.005, p=0.895 (time-performance relationship unclear). Model-based simulation tasks: r=-0.053, p=0.226 (unclear/negative). Gender difference in time-on-task during knowledge acquisition: t(2150.4)=4.79, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.19; females spent more time across all tasks (Robot Cleaner: t(506.03)=4.28, p<0.001, d=0.33; Air-Cons Control: t(494.65)=3.80, p<0.001, d=0.28; Social Activity: t(572.2)=5.01, p<0.001, d=0.41; Basketball Training: t(579.36)=4.73, p<0.001, d=0.38).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study assessed whether time-on-task predicted knowledge acquisition achievement and found that the relationship was generally unclear in both realistic (r=0.005, p=0.895) and model-based tasks (r=-0.053, p=0.226). This indicates that longer engagement time alone is not a reliable proxy for effective exploration; policy and practice should emphasize strategy quality (e.g., VOTAT/control-of-variables) and task-appropriate guidance rather than time-on-task targets.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework (MicroFIN Robot Cleaner; exploration stage) — Vietnamese university undergraduate CPS test
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge acquisition achievement (Rasch-scaled) predicted by number of observations
main_findings.performance_metrics: Realistic Robot Cleaner: number of observations positively associated with achievement at this stage r=0.110, p=0.024 (correlation reported as notable finding). Correlation between achievement and specific strategies employed was described as inconclusive (no numeric metric provided).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework data from the Vietnamese undergraduate CPS test, the study found that in the Robot Cleaner exploratory stage, the number of observations was significantly and positively associated with knowledge acquisition achievement (r=0.110, p=0.024), while correlations with specific strategy categories were inconclusive. This indicates that engagement behaviors that increase systematic sampling of the environment may support learning, but strategy taxonomy alone may not capture the mechanisms without more granular strategy measurement.

data.outcome_summary: This study investigated complex problem-solving among 589 Vietnamese undergraduate students using CPS tasks aligned with the PISA 2012 Creative Problem Solving framework, combining performance data (Rasch-scaled CPS scores from dichotomous item scoring) and process data (log-derived number of interactions, time-on-task, strategy frequencies, and spatial interaction patterns). The paper did not train machine-learning predictive models; instead, it used Rasch scaling plus Pearson correlations and t-tests to characterize relationships between engagement behaviors and achievement. Key results show that students performed better in knowledge acquisition than knowledge application (t(588)=7.33, p<0.001), and males outperformed females overall and especially in knowledge acquisition (overall t(543.67)=3.569, p<.001; d=0.30). In MicroDYN model-based tasks, more actions were weakly negatively related to knowledge acquisition (r=-0.087, p=0.04), while in the MicroFIN realistic Robot Cleaner task the association was positive (r=0.198, p<0.001). Time-on-task was generally not predictive (realistic r=0.005, p=0.895; model-based r=-0.053, p=0.226), and VOTAT-like “vary one variable” behavior (Change 1) correlated positively with achievement (r=0.343***). Limitations include a single-university convenience sample, no reported missing-data strategy, and no PV-based ILSA weighting or causal identification.
